reviewed.attack: Read Millot and Baumann (arXiv 2401.01606) in full text to check equations and Tables 2 and 3; re-ran the spike's equations at 44.1, 88.2, 176.4, 352.8 and 705.6 kHz with the same semi-implicit Euler scheme, and with classical RK4 at 352.8 kHz, to test whether the oscillation is a numerical artefact.
reviewed.finding: The oscillation is physical in the model, not numerical: at v0 = 1.5 m/s f0 is 440.86, 440.74, 440.69, 440.67 and 440.66 Hz from 44.1 to 705.6 kHz, and RK4 gives 440.65 Hz with tip amplitude within 0.3 % of the semi-implicit result; flow H2 converges to -18.4 dB. Parameters match Tables 2 and 3. Caveats: (a) Table 2 parameters were measured on a (+,-) reed (G diatonic, channel 4, Lee Oskar), and the paper itself says (-,+) and (+,-) reeds on a diatonic have different properties, so 'published harmonica-reed parameters' for the (-,+) case the spike simulates are borrowed; (b) the paper integrates with backward Euler plus a bilinear (pre-warped) reed equation and Newton-Raphson per sample, not semi-implicit Euler, so the scheme is the spike's own choice; (c) the spike sets the rest tip offset as +528 um on the upstream side, while Table 2 gives a different rest opening formula per reed type (-Δh - er/2 - es for (-,+)) in the paper's own coordinate; the sign convention was not reconciled line by line. Positive finding for the plan: the semi-implicit scheme is stable and within 0.8 cents of the converged value at plain 44.1 kHz for these parameters, so 8x oversampling is not needed for stability at this note.
reviewed.suggested_rewording: ... self-oscillates when integrated with a semi-implicit Euler scheme at 44.1 to 705.6 kHz (converged; RK4 agrees), using the Table 2 parameters, which were measured on a (+,-) reed and are borrowed for the (-,+) configuration simulated.

new_sources.title: A proposal for a minimal model of free reeds
new_sources.locator: Table 2 caption; section 3.2 paragraph after Figure 16; appendix 5.4 'Keypoints of the numerical simulations method'

reviewed.attack: Re-ran with supply held up then lowered (hysteresis), with supply raised slowly past 4 m/s after the sound had started, at five sample rates and with RK4; compared with the paper's Figures 22 and 23 and section 3.5.
reviewed.finding: (1) The 'threshold' is start-dependent: from rest the reed is silent at 1.0 m/s, but after sounding at 2.0 m/s and dropping to 1.0 m/s it keeps sounding (tip amplitude 672 um) and at 0.8 m/s still oscillates at 175 um 0.8 s later. This is the inverse (subcritical) bifurcation with hysteresis that the paper itself reports. (2) Choking at 4 m/s happens only for a fast ramp from rest (0.05 s): when the supply is raised over 0.3 s from an established 3.5 m/s sound to 4, 5 and 6 m/s the reed keeps sounding (2.6, 2.9, 3.1 mm, -13.9 to -14.5 cents). The paper's (-,+) reed sounds from about 1 to 10 m/s (Figure 22 axis). So 'at 4 m/s the reed is pushed through the plate and stops' is a property of an abrupt attack from rest, not of the supply level. (3) The pitch figures are confirmed and converged (-12.3 to -13.8 cents across sample rates) and agree in kind with the paper (the (-,+) reed plays slightly below 444 Hz, nearly independent of v0).
reviewed.suggested_rewording: In that model the onset from rest needs a supply between 1.0 and 1.5 m/s (through 30 mm2) but, once sounding, the reed keeps sounding at 1.0 m/s and below (hysteresis; inverse bifurcation, as Millot and Baumann report); the playing frequency lies about 13 cents below fr and falls slightly with supply; tip amplitude grows with supply; an abrupt attack from rest at 4 m/s or more drives the reed to a static choked position, whereas a gradual rise from an established sound to 6 m/s keeps it sounding.

new_sources.title: A proposal for a minimal model of free reeds
new_sources.locator: section 3.5 'Influence of the excitation velocity v0', Figure 22 and the bifurcation paragraph

reviewed.attack: Checked the result at five sample rates and with RK4; checked what signal the spike analyses.
reviewed.finding: Converged: flow H2 at 3.5 m/s is -9.2, -9.0, -8.9, -8.9, -8.8 dB from 44.1 to 705.6 kHz; reed H2 -43 to -54 dB. The analysed signal is the total flow u in pipe 2, which includes the pumped flow Sr*dz/dt, not the jet flow alone, and the radiated pressure of a monopole goes as du/dt (+6 dB per octave on harmonics), so the sound spectrum is brighter than the flow spectrum quoted. 'The harmonic content of the sound comes from the flow law' is an inference: the spike computes no sound, and in an instrument the downstream acoustics (comb, cover plates, hands) also shape it.
reviewed.suggested_rewording: ... while the total volume flow through the reed (jet plus pumped flow) carries strong harmonics ...; so in this model the harmonic content of the source flow comes from the nonlinear flow law, not from the reed motion.

reviewed.attack: Read the condition in the paper; extended the spike's L1 = 30 mm and 20 mm runs from 1.2 s to 4 s, because the original 30 mm result (6.6 um 'oscillation') was barely above the 5 um detection threshold.
reviewed.finding: Paper confirms: for a (-,+) reed (A < 0) the linear analysis needs 1 - V1*L2*w^2/(c0^2*S2) < 0. The spike's 30 mm case was a slowly growing transient at 1.2 s; at 4 s it saturates at 658 um, so the conclusion holds. The 20 mm case decays to 6e-12 m. Caveats: the condition is necessary from a linearised analysis with a quadratic approximation to Su, not sufficient; equivalently it says the reed frequency must lie above the Helmholtz frequency of V1 with pipe 2; onset time near the boundary exceeds one second, which matters for a playable instrument (the plan's harmonica cavity must sit well inside the condition, not near it).
reviewed.suggested_rewording: A (-,+) reed in the minimal configuration can oscillate only if V1*L2*w^2/(c0^2*S2) > 1 (a necessary condition from linear analysis); near the boundary (ratio 1.27) the onset takes more than a second.

reviewed.attack: Downloaded the Woodhouse 2021 JASA paper (author copy) and checked eqs (1) to (4) symbol by symbol.
reviewed.finding: All four formulas and the constants match exactly (section II A, eqs 1 to 4), including the statement that air damping dominates low modes and bending damping high modes. Limits stated in the source: eq. (1) holds only when |Y/Y0| is small; the air term is quoted from Fletcher and Rossing (1998), so the two are not independent. For wound strings (bouzouki and mandolin bass courses) the solid-wire air and bending terms need an effective density and diameter, and the source notes extra friction damping for overwound strings; the plan must not apply the plain-wire forms to wound strings unmodified. No second independent readable source found.
reviewed.suggested_rewording: ... (Woodhouse 2021, eqs 1-4; valid for |Y/Y0| << 1; air term after Fletcher and Rossing 1998; for wound strings an effective d and rho must be chosen and friction losses are extra).

reviewed.attack: Read spike S04 line by line; checked the coupling matrix algebra; examined the 'strong coupling' case against the exceptional point; read Woodhouse 2021 introduction.
reviewed.finding: The algebra is right (one string alone decays with eta_i + eta_b, the symmetric mode with eta_i + 2*eta_b). The source confirms the symmetric/antisymmetric picture. Caveats: (a) the coupling is purely resistive; Weinreich's results with a reactive bridge admittance (mode repulsion rather than locking) are not exercised; (b) with the spike's numbers the exceptional point (frequency locking boundary) is at about 3.46 cents, so the '3c strong coupling' case sits just inside it, and locking needs mistuning below about eta_b*f/ (2 ln2/1200 ...) i.e. a few cents at eta_b = 2e-3; (c) one polarisation only: Woodhouse and others attribute double decay also to the two polarisations of a single string, which the model omits; (d) the beat test is nearly tautological (sum of two sinusoids beats at their difference).
reviewed.suggested_rewording: ... with purely resistive coupling the two frequencies lock when the mistuning is below the coupling (about 3.5 cents at eta_b = 2e-3, 660 Hz); a reactive bridge admittance repels them instead; one polarisation only.

new_sources.title: A necessary condition for double-decay envelopes in stringed instruments
new_sources.locator: section I, paragraphs 1-2; section II A eqs (1)-(4)

reviewed.attack: Checked whether the spike tests modal synthesis against anything independent; compared the eigen-expansion with a matrix exponential across mistunings including the exceptional point.
reviewed.finding: The spike computes its envelope from the eigen-decomposition and never compares it with an independent solution, so as evidence it is circular. My check: the modal sum agrees with expm(i*Omega*t) to 6e-13 across 1 to 8 cents, but near the exceptional point (about 3.46 cents) cond(V) reaches 45 and modal amplitudes reach 16 times the pluck with cancellation; exactly at the exceptional point the matrix is defective and the response contains t*exp(...) terms, which no sum of exponentials represents. In single-precision real-time code this costs precision. 'Exactly' holds for diagonalisable linear systems only.
reviewed.suggested_rewording: Modal synthesis reproduces a linear coupled model exactly whenever the system matrix is diagonalisable; near the locking boundary the modal amplitudes become large and cancel, so the implementation should detect near-defective pairs (or simulate the 2x2 block directly).

missing_claims.claim: The reed equations stay stable and accurate at the host sample rate without oversampling for the parameters used (semi-implicit Euler at 44.1 kHz: f0 within 0.8 cent and amplitude within 2 % of the 705.6 kHz result at fr = 444 Hz); stability for high reeds (fr up to about 2 to 3 kHz, very stiff short reeds) and for small Su has not been tested.
missing_claims.why_it_matters: Decides oversampling factor and CPU budget for up to about 40 reeds sounding (accordion Master register, harmonica chords).
missing_claims.evidence: Adversarial re-run of S03 at 44.1-705.6 kHz (this round); high reeds untested.

missing_claims.claim: The free-reed onset is hysteretic (inverse bifurcation): sound starts above one supply level and persists below it.
missing_claims.why_it_matters: Bellows and breath mapping, note-off behaviour and tests that assert a threshold must allow for hysteresis.
missing_claims.evidence: Millot and Baumann 2024 section 3.5; S03 re-run with supply lowered to 1.0 m/s.

missing_claims.claim: Silent or decaying reed and string states must be flushed to zero (flush-to-zero/denormals-are-zero, e.g. JUCE ScopedNoDenormals, plus explicit silence detection) to avoid denormal CPU spikes.
missing_claims.why_it_matters: The reed integrator decays geometrically to 1e-12 m and below when silent (L1 = 20 mm run reached 6e-12 m), which reaches the subnormal range in float32 within seconds on many voices.
missing_claims.evidence: S03 re-run decay; standard real-time audio practice (no Tier 1 source read in this round).

missing_claims.claim: The per-sample flow law divides by alpha*Su(x); Su has a floor only through hmin, and the jet velocity can be large when the reed is inside the plate, so the real-time code needs a guarded division and no allocation or table rebuild on the audio thread.
missing_claims.why_it_matters: Real-time safety of the reed integration at audio rate.
missing_claims.evidence: reed_sim.py lines computing vj; Su_min = 1.4 mm2 in output.json.
